items.title: What #BookTok taught us about building an audience from zero
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: Sixteen months, one novelist, no existing audience. The parts of the approach that transfer to any personal brand.
body:
How do you introduce an author to people who have never read her books?

That was the question behind our work with novelist Caroline Montague. When we began, Caroline had around 5,000 Instagram followers and no TikTok presence. She had a body of work and a life full of stories, but her social channels weren’t yet giving people enough opportunity to discover either.

We made TikTok the focus, building a video-led approach around Caroline’s writing, reading and everyday surroundings. BookTok gave that work a relevant community to speak to.

The experience offers useful lessons for any founder, creative or brand building an audience from the beginning.
Q:The mistake most personal brands make is treating the platform as a distribution channel for something that already exists. It is not. It is the thing itself.
H:Start with the room, not the audience

Start with the community you want to join

Before deciding what to post, consider whose attention you are hoping to earn—and what those people already enjoy talking about.

For an author, “people who buy books” is only a starting point. There are conversations around favourite characters, reading habits, historical settings, writing routines and the feeling of finishing a book you wish had lasted longer.

Each offers a different way into the same subject.

This is a useful exercise for brands too. A clothing label can explore the decisions people make when getting dressed. A movement studio can address the uncertainty of attending a first class. A founder can explain the product detail they kept changing until it felt right.

Look for a conversation you can contribute to meaningfully. That gives your content a clearer purpose than simply announcing that your business exists.

Give people a way to discover the person behind the work

With Caroline, the creative direction extended beyond book announcements. Her home, reading and writing routine became part of the content itself, giving viewers more ways to encounter her as a person.

For a personal brand, this raises an important question: what can someone connect with before they are ready to buy?

They might be interested in your perspective, recognise something in your routine or enjoy watching how you approach your work. Those points of connection give a new viewer a reason to explore further.

You do not have to share every part of your life. Choose details that help people understand your work and that you feel comfortable returning to publicly.

Make each video understandable to someone new

When you are building an audience from zero, your content needs to work for people with no prior knowledge of you.

Watch a draft through that person’s eyes. Is it clear who is speaking? Does the opening establish something interesting? Can the viewer understand the subject without reading several previous posts?

For an author, an opening such as “A detail I had to research before writing this scene” introduces a complete idea. “Another update on the book” assumes an existing interest.

The same principle applies to businesses. Show the question, decision or demonstration early enough for a new viewer to understand why it is worth watching.

These are possible approaches, rather than scripts every account should follow. The opening still needs to sound like the person delivering it.

Build a world you can keep creating within

A launch provides a natural reason to post, but an audience needs something to return to between announcements.

Think about the subjects your brand can explore repeatedly without saying the same thing. For a writer, that could include research, reading and the process of developing a story. For a product founder, it might include design decisions, customer questions and how the product fits into everyday life.

A useful content theme should be specific enough to be recognisable and broad enough to support different episodes.

Try listing ten genuinely different ideas beneath each proposed theme. If you struggle after the first two, it may be a single post rather than a lasting part of your strategy.

Give one platform a clear role

For Caroline, TikTok was the main focus of the strategy. That decision gave the work a clear centre.

For other brands, the right starting platform may be different. The practical lesson is to decide where you can give the audience and the creative process enough attention.

Consider where relevant conversations are happening, which formats suit your subject and what your team can realistically produce. Then define how your other channels will support that work.

You can adapt an idea across platforms while still considering how someone will encounter it in each place. A consistent brand does not require every post to be identical.

Learn from attention without making it the only goal

When reviewing content, ask what the response helps you understand.

Did people become curious about the person or product? Were they asking relevant questions? Did they visit the profile, explore the website or return for another instalment?

Views can tell you that a piece travelled. Other signals help you assess whether it reached people who might develop a lasting interest.

For an author, that interest might eventually lead someone to explore a book. For a service business, it might lead to an enquiry. Neither should be assumed from a large view count alone.

Give people a reason to come inside

Our work with Caroline centred on making her world more accessible to people who had not discovered it yet.

That is a useful place to begin with any social strategy. What is interesting, useful or distinctive about your business that a stranger could appreciate today? How can you express it in a way they will understand?

Answer those questions well, and your content has something substantial to build on.

Explore our work with Caroline Montague or talk to Glasshouse about building your social presence.
